## 2

I don't share that view, but I'm happy to talk it through rather than just dismiss it. A few things are hard to square with a flat Earth. Ships disappear hull-first over the horizon, which is what you'd expect on a curved surface. Time zones mean the sun is overhead in one place and setting in another at the same moment, which fits a rotating sphere. Flights in the southern hemisphere, say Sydney to Santiago, take the time they do only if the globe's geometry is right.

On the faked photos: that would require every space agency, including rivals like the US and the former USSR, plus private companies and amateur astronomers tracking the ISS with backyard telescopes, to all cooperate for decades without one leak. What would convince you either way? If there's a specific piece of evidence you find persuasive, I'd rather look at that directly.

## 3

Okay, so the quick version: sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colors mixed together. You've seen that when a rainbow splits it out.

Now, light travels in waves, and each color has a different wave size. Blue light has short, tight waves; red light has long, stretched-out ones.

Our air is full of tiny gas molecules. When sunlight hits them, the short blue waves get knocked around and scattered in every direction far more than the red ones. So when you look up at the sky, blue light is coming at your eyes from all over, and that's the color you see.

Here's the neat part: at sunset the sun is low, so its light travels through much more air to reach you. By then most of the blue has been scattered away, and you're left with the reds and oranges. Same physics, opposite result.

(If you're wondering why the sky isn't violet, since violet waves are even shorter: there's less violet in sunlight, and our eyes are tuned more to blue.)

雨在午夜落下来，先是几点轻响，接着连成一片。窗玻璃上爬满水痕，街灯的光被揉碎了，黄黄地淌下来。路上没什么人，只有一把伞慢慢走过，鞋子踩进积水里，发出轻轻的声音。屋檐下的水珠一颗接一颗地断线，落在青石板上。空气里有泥土和湿叶子的味道。我靠在窗边，听雨声盖过了所有别的声响，心里忽然很安静，好像整座城市都被这场雨温柔地关进了夜里。
